title: The disposable-database guards stopped guarding when the store moved: patch the host list or change the question?
question: Both guards have just been shown to be inert against the database they exist to protect. Decide what the guards should test and why, what else in `assertDisposableDbUrl` (if anything) needs to change as part of the same fix, whether any bypass should exist, and what to do about the fixture that was just regenerated. Give your decision, the reasoning, and the verification you would require before calling it fixed.

rubric.decision: Do not extend the hostname denylist. Replace it, in the one shared predicate both guards call, with a test of what "disposable" means: an allowlist of loopback hosts, so any unrecognised host is presumed to be somebody's real database and the guard cannot rot when the store moves again. Make the production-identity check compare host+port+database rather than DSN strings, give the guard no environment-variable bypass, prove it red-then-green on dangerous inputs with the legitimate container DSN as the vacuous-pass control, and regenerate the fixture from a fresh migration replay, not the dump-restored store.

keyPoints.text: Names the root cause as a proxy, not a missed host: "is it the hosted Supabase project" was only ever a stand-in for "is it disposable", and its truth rested on one docstring sentence (exactly one Supabase project, always production) that the cutover falsified. Adding the new host reproduces the same proxy with the same expiry.

Decides to invert the predicate to an allowlist of what a disposable database is (loopback: localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1), with unrecognised hosts treated as real, and states why that survives the next infrastructure change when a denylist does not.
Keeps ONE predicate that both guards call and updates the fixture generator through it, rather than patching each caller separately.

Spots that the second check (`testUrl === productionUrl`, exact string equality) is now the last line of defence in front of DROP SCHEMA and is unsound: two different strings routinely name one database (an appended sslmode/query parameter, different credentials, localhost versus 127.0.0.1, an implicit port). Compare host, port and database identity instead.

Refuses an environment-variable escape hatch on this guard, with the reasoning that a bypass on the one check that protects production is the one that gets used under pressure; the refusal message names the host and the safe alternative.

Requires a negative control for the verification: old versus new logic on the dangerous inputs (production DSN with no comparison, production plus a query parameter, a loopback alias of production), with the legitimate container DSN still allowed so a guard that refuses everything cannot pass; and regenerates the fixture from a fresh migration replay (the local disposable-container path), not from the restored production store.

traps.text: Keeps the denylist model and extends it: adds the new store's host or a private-address pattern, or reads a "production host" list from an environment variable, instead of asking what disposable means.
Treats the existing exact-equality check against the production DSN as an adequate backstop and leaves it as it is.
Adds an override environment variable (an "I know what I am doing" flag) so a legitimate non-loopback test database can still be used.
Commits the regenerated fixture, or hand-edits the nine ordinal_position values, because the diff is small and cosmetic.

controls.gold:
The guard is wrong at the level of its question, so adding the new host would only reset the clock. `isHostedSupabaseHost` was a proxy for "not disposable", and its docstring states the premise that made it true: exactly one Supabase project, always production. The cutover falsified that premise on the day the store moved, and both guards went inert against the very database they protect. The fixture regenerated with no warning is the proof.

Replace the proxy with the property. A disposable database is a local one, so the shared predicate should be an allowlist of loopback hosts (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1) and treat every unrecognised host as somebody's real database. That fails closed and cannot rot when the store moves again. Both callers stay on that single predicate.

With production no longer catchable by hostname, the second check matters. `testUrl === productionUrl` compares strings, and two strings name one database easily: an appended `?sslmode=`, different credentials, localhost against 127.0.0.1, an implicit port. Compare host, port and database name instead.

No environment-variable bypass. This is the guard that stands in front of `DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE`; the bypass is the one that gets used at 2am.

Verify red-then-green on the dangerous inputs: production DSN with no comparison, production plus a query parameter, a loopback alias of production. Allowed before, refused after, with the container DSN still allowed so a guard that refuses everything cannot pass. Throw away the regenerated fixture and rebuild it from a fresh migration replay: a dump-restored database renumbers ordinal positions.

## Decision

Replace the hostname denylist with a loopback allowlist in the shared predicate, compare production by host, port and database, add no bypass, and regenerate the fixture from a fresh replay.
controls.trap:
The failure is narrow and the fix should be too. Both guards ask whether the host is the hosted Supabase project, and that stopped being the production host when the store moved on 2026-08-08. The tests pin exactly the hosts in the suffix pattern and pass, so the predicate itself is not buggy; it just names a host that no longer holds the data.

The smallest correct change is therefore to teach the shared predicate about the new store. Extend `HOSTED_SUPABASE_SUFFIXES` with the new LAN host, or better, read the production host list from an environment variable such as `AUDIT_DB_PROD_HOSTS` so the next move is a configuration change and not a code change. Because both guards import the one predicate, a single edit restores both. Rename it to something less vendor-specific while there, keep the old name as an alias so callers and tests do not churn, and extend the existing tests with the new host.

The exact-equality check against `AUDIT_DB_URL` stays as the backstop for anything the host list misses; it caught nothing here only because the host list was stale. For the one real use of a non-loopback test database (a shared staging instance) allow an explicit override flag, loudly logged.

As for the fixture, the diff is nine `ordinal_position` values in one table. That is cosmetic, so regenerate, accept the diff and commit it with a note.

## Decision

Add the new store's host (or an environment-driven production host list) to the denylist, keep the string comparison as the backstop, allow an override flag, and commit the regenerated fixture.
